How We Reported This Story

How We Counted Incidents

We found and vetted cases from a number of sources, including English- and Spanish-language social media, DHS statements, court records and local news reports, in addition to our own reporting. We included an incident in our dataset only if we could find at least two sources for it. For additional details about the incident, like whether crowd control weapons were used, we accepted one source in some cases.

When DHS provided a response specific to an incident — including about whether it happened or the circumstances under which it happened — we noted that response in cases for which we offered detail beyond a simple count of detained citizens. DHS responses that generically denied ever detaining citizens or that are proven inaccurate by our reporting were not included.

As with our count a year ago, most of the detained Americans on our list fell into two broad categories. The first is Americans who were held because agents questioned their citizenship. This time, we found more than a hundred such cases. The second category is Americans arrested by immigration agents after being accused of assaulting or impeding officers at protests or during immigration arrests of others. In that category, we tallied roughly 300 Americans. In many of these cases, the government accused but never charged these individuals with assault. Sometimes agents detained people because of questions about their citizenship but later accused them of crimes. While public attention often focuses on ICE, the immigration dragnet often relied on officers from agencies across the government.

Since the government itself does not track these cases, our list is almost certainly an undercount. Except in a few cases in which DHS itself confirmed detentions, we only counted citizens we were able to individually identify. So, for example, while witnesses estimate as many as 200 citizens were detained in an Idaho raid last fall, we were only able to identify 30 individuals by time of publication. We encountered the same issues for many smaller raids and protests, such as a raid of a food plant in Cato, New York ; protesters detained by ICE at Delaney Hall in Newark, New Jersey; and a raid of a Hyundai-LG plant in Ellabell, Georgia .

ICE itself occasionally has stated higher numbers than we were able to confirm: It told Congress that 131 citizens were arrested for assaulting, obstructing or interfering this year in Minnesota’s Metro Surge. It didn’t name them. We cataloged fewer than a hundred.

We tagged each case with details like whether a minor was detained or a citizen was held after filming. Another trend we tracked was citizens held for more than a day without access to a lawyer or their family. When multiple citizens were detained in one incident or sometimes on the same day and city, we grouped them together.

Because we focused on the expanded presence of immigration agents in American communities, we restricted our count to warrantless arrests that took place outside of airports and away from the borders, where immigration agents have long had more authority. We also excluded cases of Americans who were arrested after a judicial warrant.

We did not include incidents where an agent shot, tackled or pepper-sprayed a citizen but didn’t detain them.

We also did not include immigration protesters arrested by police who were only enforcing local laws. We did, however, include some cases involving police working with immigration agents. We still have little visibility into how many citizens have been detained by police deputized to act as immigration agents.

We also found reports of more than 30 Americans who felt racially profiled by immigration agents, but we did not include them in our database because it was not clear they were held against their will.

How We Counted and Reviewed Court Cases

We searched every named adult in our list to see if they were charged with a federal crime in relation to their detention. We conducted searches, using several name combinations for people with double names or compound names, in federal district courts through the online platform PACER. We looked for a criminal case filed within two months of the noted date of a person’s detention in the judicial district in which the detention happened. We then noted whether we found charges, what the charges were, and whether the person involved was sentenced or had their case dismissed or discharged.

How We Chose the Videos in This Report

We reviewed hundreds of videos of federal agents detaining American citizens across the country. While that included body camera footage, news clippings and helicopter footage, the vast majority of videos were made by bystanders and shared over social media. Many of the videos went viral and were recirculated across the internet by a range of third-party accounts. They touch on everyday American life in a range of settings, including workplaces, homes, protests, car washes, suburban sidewalks and the interiors of vehicles.

We tagged each video with how clearly it shows the incident and whether the citizen detained was clearly visible. We then categorized the videos by the kind of conduct they show, such as citizens being detained after recording. We provided DHS an opportunity to respond to each of the videos we included.

Given the violence and upsetting subject matter of many of the videos in this report, we also chose to provide an option for readers to turn off the videos.

We did not alter videos, nor did we add watermarks, blur faces or overlay captions on videos unless otherwise noted. Videos that include captions or watermarks are shown as they were obtained.

stories.body:
ProPublica reporter Jake Pearson immersed himself in the world of online sports betting on DraftKings to test the limits of the company’s “responsible gaming” safeguards. Here are five things he learned.

Online gambling has surged in the U.S. since the Supreme Court allowed states to legalize sports betting in 2018, prompting public health concerns about gambling addiction and calls for stricter consumer protections. Online sportsbooks such as DraftKings and FanDuel have touted “responsible gaming” features as evidence that they are taking appropriate steps to protect consumers from spiraling out of control.

Reporter Jake Pearson put these safeguards to the test. Bankrolled by ProPublica, he mimicked the betting patterns of a problem gambler for 10 weeks, consulting a panel of addiction specialists, recovering gambling addicts and professional sports bettors for advice.

He found that the safety features were overpowered by the app’s product design and promotions that pushed him to continue gambling.

Pearson detailed his entire journey, which you can read here . Here are five takeaways from his investigation.

1. Sports betting is ubiquitous. The industry relies on very active losers.

Today, nearly a quarter of all Americans , and half of men ages 18 to 49, say they have an active sportsbook account, according to the Siena Research Institute. But that rapid growth has come with consequences: About a quarter of active sportsbook account holders surveyed by the organization this year said that they’d lost enough on a bet that they’d have trouble meeting their financial obligations.

Gamblers who lose frequently are the bettors sportsbooks are most interested in, Matthew Gaskell, a British psychologist and expert on gambling addiction, said. Gaskell noted that a relatively small number of active losers account for a substantial amount of sportsbooks’ revenue.

A 2024 study out of Connecticut found that 1.8% of problem gamblers in the state accounted for 51% of sports betting revenue .

What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out.

If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files.

DraftKings says its responsible gaming system provides adequate safeguards to protect customers from spiraling out of control. “I think as a business, as an industry, we’re doing a good job of educating people, of raising awareness, of making tools and resources available, of monitoring accounts,” Lori Kalani, DraftKings’ chief responsible gaming officer, told Pearson.

But policymakers aren’t so sure. Lawmakers from Colorado to Massachusetts are now proposing stricter consumer protections.

2. DraftKings has adopted responsible gaming tools. They require users to opt in, limiting their effectiveness.

DraftKings’ responsible gambling safeguards include in-app notifications that encourage gamblers to take a break after they’ve lost money and “time reminders” that tell users how long they’ve been on the app. The app also features a responsible gaming center that allows users to set a budget, track their spending or opt into tools like those that allow them to limit the amount of time and money they spend in a 24-hour period or enact more severe restrictions such as a multiday “cool off.”

But this system largely relies on users to have the wherewithal to opt into the tools — something that experts say can be difficult for someone struggling with gambling addiction.

DraftKings told Pearson that if a customer’s behavior raises too many red flags, the company will proactively close an account. Yet it wouldn’t specify how often this actually happens.

Pearson’s experiment mimicked the behavior of a problem gambler to see when — and if — the company’s safeguards would stop him. The first in-app responsible gaming prompt Pearson received came more than a week after he began gambling on the NBA playoffs, when he’d already lost roughly what a minimum-wage worker in New York City earns in a month. It told him that he’d hit $2,500 or more in deposits and said to “visit our Responsible Gaming Center anytime to set limits for yourself and access tools for safer play.”

But the app’s warning wasn’t triggered by Pearson’s reckless betting. It was legally required. When New York legalized mobile sports betting in 2023, lawmakers required the apps to notify users when they hit $2,500 in total deposits. The pop-up gave Pearson two options: set limits or “I understand.” He clicked the latter and was back in action.

Even as Pearson exhibited red flag after red flag, according to our panel of experts, his subsequent warnings from the app followed the same pattern.

DraftKings says millions of customers have visited its responsible gaming center, but the little data available publicly suggests only a small percentage opt into these tools. Just over 8% of active DraftKings users in Massachusetts were using them as of April, a company official told state regulators this summer. The official added the number was trending up.

Kalani says her 51-person team manually reviews user accounts suspected of problem gambling. Yet even after Pearson deposited $21,600 into his account in less than eight weeks and exhibited just about every sign of compulsive gambling, he didn’t register for a manual review under the company’s criteria.

3. The design of online sports betting platforms can encourage users to gamble more.

Online gambling companies have created sophisticated technology products designed to squeeze maximum engagement out of users, just as social media companies like Meta did years earlier with users of Facebook and Instagram, according to Darragh McGee, a researcher at the University of Bath.

Indeed, Pearson found that the app’s design encouraged him to keep betting.

As he gambled more, he found that the app’s quick-tap deposit buttons increased automatically, making it even easier to mindlessly transfer large sums from his bank into his DraftKings account. And while DraftKings’ safety warnings were sporadic, he was getting up to six push notifications a day notifying him of rewards and betting opportunities.

DraftKings told Pearson it sent him 32 responsible gambling prompts over 10 weeks of gambling, including emails that every DraftKings customer gets. Pearson counted in-app notifications about his betting 14 out of the 71 days he gambled on the app.

4. Perks can also help encourage users to bet more.

DraftKings, like many other sportsbooks, also offers VIP programs that give users perks, including free bets and concert tickets. After Pearson lost $1,800 betting on basketball in one night, chasing his losses with increasingly long-shot bets, he was invited to audition to become a DraftKings VIP. After only three weeks and $5,800 in deposits on the app, Pearson was formally accepted into DraftKings’ VIP program, which assigned him a personal concierge.

That VIP host told Pearson that he would be “keeping an eye out for opportunities and perks tailored specifically” to his account, plus “reminders about Responsible Gaming.” Company representatives offer VIPs special incentives to continue gambling, such as “bonus bets” (free one-time bets using house money) and “deposit matches” (extra house money called DK Dollars that come along with new deposits).

Pearson found that the program rewarded riskier bets. The more money users spend on long-odds wagers, the quicker they accumulate credits needed to “advance” to higher tiers that offer better perks.

Less than a week after Pearson opted into a three-day “cool-off” period — after losing several thousand dollars betting on tennis — Pearson contacted his VIP representative, who helped facilitate his largest deposit match to date: juicing a $5,000 deposit with an extra $1,250 in free DK Dollars.

5. Online gamblers are left to regulate themselves. Experts say more limits are needed.

Lawmakers face a public policy dilemma: While online gambling generates billions of dollars in tax revenue, research shows that gambling disorder diagnoses are rising in states that have legalized.

In New York, sportsbooks like DraftKings have to submit a “problem-gaming plan” to the state regulator but the law leaves the specifics of it up to the companies. The plan must include, among other things, procedures “for identifying users with suspected or known problem-gaming behavior” and for “providing information to users concerning problem-gaming identification and resources.” The exact details are unclear because such plans are not publicly available. (A DraftKings spokesperson wouldn’t provide a copy, and Pearson’s request for it under the state’s open records law with the gaming commission is under review.)

Other countries have already taken aggressive steps to regulate online sportsbooks’ marketing practices and advertisements. But in the U.S., the industry has actively opposed proposed reforms on the federal and state levels — and even seeded a political action committee with $41 million to influence elections this year.

Rob Minnick, a recovering gambling addict and one of the experts we consulted, said that the framework for protecting consumers shouldn’t be entrusted to a publicly traded company that’s driven to grow revenue.

DraftKings told Pearson that all 5,000-plus of its employees are trained on responsible gaming every year and that it’s “not a side initiative. It is embedded across our business and essential to DraftKings’ long-term sustainability.”

“The system worked the way it was supposed to,” Kalani told Pearson.

Critics say that’s the problem.

Every local government election season , South Africans are handed the same menu. They hear from councillor hopefuls that they will repair potholes, stop water outages and power cuts, and improve refuse collection. Politicians campaign on service delivery as though it were the only job of local government. It isn’t.

Service delivery is what happens after the real decisions have already been made: where people are allowed to live, work and move, at what density, and on whose land. That decision is town planning, and it is the most under-discussed, under-resourced, and consequential function of South African local government.

Read more: South African floods wreaked havoc because people are forced to live in disaster prone areas

I have spent a career studying how municipalities plan, or fail to plan, for the cities their residents actually live in. My book, Spatial Planning in Service Delivery: Towards Distributive Justice in South Africa , and the research I lead as South Africa’s SARChI Chair for Inclusive Cities shows that in many municipalities, citizens and politicians argue over visible problems – such as traffic, housing shortages, informal settlements and poor services – but pay too little attention to urban planning, which can either cause these problems or help prevent them.

In this article I suggest seven priority areas where residents of South African towns and cities can take action before the local government elections on 5 November 2026. These are the areas where public pressure is most likely to change how decisions are made.

Seven ways residents can push municipalities to plan better

Based on what I have observed, residents and councillors can use existing laws, budgets and public meetings to push municipalities to plan before the next crisis instead of reacting afterwards.

1. Push for the Spatial Development Framework and use it

Every municipality should have a Spatial Development Framework showing where development should take place and how roads, water and other services will support it. Residents can demand to see it and hold councillors to it. This will help stop developments from being approved simply because land is cheap or developers apply pressure, even when services have not been planned or funded.

Read more: In their rush to become “global”, cities risk creating spatial apartheid

Right now, residents don’t use this lever. Parliament heard in 2024 that only 51% of municipalities complied with their own Spatial Development Framework. If you live in South Africa, no matter where, ask your councillor for this document. Check when it was last reviewed, and which decisions were made in line with it.

2. Ask about capacity, not only corruption

Residents are right to suspect corruption when a planning decision favours the wrong person. But in smaller and rural municipalities, the more common and more fixable problem is that there is simply no one there to do the job. Knowing which one they are dealing with changes what they demand: corruption must be investigated, but an empty desk needs a budget line and a hiring freeze lifted. Residents should ask how many qualified planners their municipality employs.

3. Watch the Municipal Planning Tribunal

South Africa’s Spatial Planning and Land Use Management Act moved rezoning decisions from provincial government down to municipal tribunals. This was a democratic gain in principle, since decisions now sit closer to the people they affect. It means that residents can find out exactly who approved the development next door, and appeal against the decision.

Read more: Cape Town taxi strike exposes a deeply unequal city – and the legacy of apartheid

Left unwatched, that same power invites trouble. Cape Town’s Municipal Planning Tribunal has recently faced allegations that it changed its planning bylaw so tribunal members could take a short break after their 10 year terms ended, and then return, potentially eroding the tribunal’s independence. Residents should ask who sits on their tribunal, how they are appointed, and how their decisions are published and appealed.

4. Upgrade informal settlements, instead of wishing them away

South Africa is short of between 2.1 million and 2.6 million homes. More than two million households live in over 4,000 informal settlements. In several major cities, municipal planners now acknowledge that most people who need housing are living in informal settlements rather than waiting for formal houses elsewhere.

Read more: No space for culture: ‘matchbox housing’ leaves residents unable to honour customs in a South African town

Municipalities need to plan around this reality instead of treating informal settlements as temporary problems to be removed. This means spending more on water, toilets, electricity and roads where people already live, rather than building new housing on undeveloped land far from jobs and public transport. Residents should ask what percentage of their municipality’s housing budget is spent on upgrading existing informal settlements and what percentage goes towards new housing developments. The answer shows where the council’s priorities lie.

5. Make land use and transport planning talk to each other

South Africa’s transport plans promise bus routes and development close to public transport. But municipal transport and land departments often work separately. When thousands of homes are approved without better transport, poorer residents pay through longer, more expensive journeys.

Residents can ask whether their municipality’s development and transport plans are linked and whether the two departments make decisions together.

6. Plan for who actually uses the city

Spatial planning was historically designed to meet the needs of a male commuter travelling in a straight line to a single workplace. That isn’t how most women, caregivers or informal traders move: their trips are multi-stop, off-peak, and safety-conscious. Conventional planning ignores this.

Read more: Race still divides South Africa – study shows little transformation in new suburbs in country’s economic hub

My research shows that street lighting, clear lines of sight, safe paths and the placement of facilities such as toilet blocks and taxi ranks are central to public safety. Residents who lobby for these will be helping cities set up safer areas that are easier to walk around with a child or a trolley. Of every new development, the question must be asked if it was designed around how women and informal traders actually move, or only around vehicle traffic counts.

7. Inclusive planning is not a wish list

In South Africa, municipalities have Integrated Development Plans , where the local council sets out its budget to cover all upgrades and service delivery. Residents can give their input at meetings about these plans and hold council to them. When a plan says that upgrading informal settlements is a priority, that is not bureaucratic language. It is a commitment citizens can quote back, line item by line item, at the next budget meeting.

What needs to happen next

For South Africa to improve its towns and cities, municipalities must employ qualified planners, fund this work properly, make departments plan together and publish clear reasons for development decisions.

Read more: Legal tools exist to protect South Africa’s city ecosystems: it’s up to councils to use them

Residents should ask not only when a pothole will be repaired, but why a development was approved, who approved it, which plan guided the decision and how it will be carried out.

Councillors must treat town planning as a major public responsibility because it determines where people live, how they travel and who has access to jobs and services.

stories.body:
How the United States abandoned the future.

Simon Curtis is an associate professor in International Relations at the University of Surrey, and a WISC Global Fellow at the Development Research Institute at New York University.

Ian Klaus is the founding director of Carnegie Endowment for International Peace California Center.

They are co-authors of “The Belt and Road City: Geopolitics, Urbanization, and China’s Search for a New International Order” (2024, Yale University Press).

The application of power, especially for Great Powers, is an exercise in time. In an auspicious year — the 250th since its founding — the United States has looked back to its revolutionary past but has shown little indication of developing a clear vision for its future. And with little apparent inclination to do so, rarely has the country seemed more adrift in the flow of history. This comes at a bad time. China’s rise has given the United States a strategic competitor intent on building its own version of tomorrow.

As the Trump administration uses its second term to try to flex the sinews of American might, the sources of American power have never seemed less well understood. The sense of purpose and destiny, and the vision and confidence of previous generations, have been replaced by confusion, division and a loss of moral clarity. Many truths once held to be self-evident are now questioned. Perhaps what has been most keenly lost is the sense that the wellsprings of national strength come from thinking intergenerationally and harnessing the power of the future, both in terms of planning and rhetoric.

But this is the wrong moment to abandon future generations. China has been preparing for decades to rival the United States in shaping the institutions and architecture of international order — first slowly and cautiously, and now increasingly assertively. China has been playing a long geopolitical game; one the United States is currently losing. In fact, it is essentially sitting out the game, trapped in nostalgia and short-termism, as China consciously builds institutions and infrastructures designed to project power across decades.

The real contest between China and the United States is not the surface froth of conflict over tariffs, shifting military capabilities, or even the development of frontier technologies like artificial intelligence or clean energy. It is a deeper and slower contest over who offers the most compelling vision of the future, and who can bring that vision into being.

The Loss Of The Future

One of the most striking features of the contemporary moment in the United States, and in the West more generally, is the sense of temporal disorientation. Once, dreams of building a better tomorrow powered the United States to victory in the Cold War. For the West, a strand of history did end with the fall of the Berlin Wall, just not in the way we expected. From 1989 onward, rather than the unending triumph of a liberal order, the West faced a strange series of crises through which it lost the historical thread altogether.

The Cold War and its most symbolic moments were an intergenerational game. The United States once reached for the stars with state-guided Cold War technological moonshots, built the architecture of a new liberal international order and defended it with a sense of intergenerational collective mission, and shaped cities and infrastructures around the world with the power of its economic model. Today, the U.S. is unmoored from that sense of historical destiny.

Much of this disorientation can be traced to cultural changes in the fabric of American society. Among them is its cultural orientation to time. This temporal disorientation takes multiple forms — but in each the future becomes opaque.

The Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement that swept Donald Trump to power began as a reaction to the failed promises of globalization, and discontent over the priorities of elites and their failures to address the concerns of everyday Americans. But as its name suggests, its orientation to time is deeply nostalgic; a wistful longing for some poorly articulated and mythical past. Part of MAGA’s failure in government stems from its lack of a compelling future-oriented vision for either domestic or international society.

But the roots of America’s problems in articulating a compelling future go far beyond MAGA. It is part of a broader crisis of time that the West has wrestled with throughout modernity. For many decades now, the political and economic culture seems trapped in a perpetual present that emphasizes short-term cycles: two-year midterm electoral cycles, four-year turnarounds in administrations whose legislative achievements are immediately unpicked by the next regime, quarterly business cycles that curtail long-term investment, 24-hour news cycles, even the rapid-fire video reels that characterize social media consumption today are but the latest manifestation of a long trend.

“The real contest between China and the United States is … a deeper and slower contest over who offers the most compelling vision of the future, and who can bring that vision into being.”

Prior to the end of the Cold War, the cultural critic Frederic Jameson sought to chart and diagnose our more recent confusion in time: the lost threads of historical narrative, the temporal dislocation and stasis of our politics. When Jameson described the cultural condition of postmodernity, he was describing a collective loss of confidence in the futures that modernity once promised; its productive energies now exhausted, history now but a mosaic and collage constructed selectively by the powerful, collective purpose dissolved in an acid of consumerist images and desires, the idea of building a future utopia no longer something that we can believe in without irony. For decades this state of stasis was undisturbed by a significant external threat or real geopolitical competitor, and so its corrosive effects were overlooked. Both time and the rare moment of unipolar power that emerged in the 1990s were squandered.

Now two such challenges disturb this malaise: the rise of China and the existential threat of climate change. And yet the seemingly permanent constraint on the temporal horizon is effectively neutering the West’s ability to meet either challenge.

Cycles Of Decay & Renewal

We needn’t be so hard on Americans. As the Cameroonian historian Achille Mbembe has noted , the West at large has foreclosed on the idea of any world to come or any imagined future. Exit is impossible, he winks in French; the longue durée is a dead idea. But of course, most Western powers are not great powers, and their roles in geopolitics — even when united in suprajurisdictions like the European Union — don’t rival the world-shaping power of the United States.

But China’s role does. Unlike the United States today, China builds its geopolitical strategies over decades. Its one-party state rolls on in pursuit of an international environment that better reflects its own domestic values and priorities, unperturbed by the political or economic storms of the present, or the vicissitudes of democratic politics. Democracies must find a way to somehow match the ability of China to dictate a geopolitical strategy that unfolds over decades if they are to build new institutions that successfully compete in the long game.

Equally disconcerting has been the eruption, at the margins of our consciousness and culture, of the concept of deep time and the realization that our societies and economies are intrinsically entangled with the systems of the natural world; that the Anthropocene is a reality that any sustainable future must come to terms with, and that untrammeled consumption and growth bring with them their own reckonings.

The deep time of the Anthropocene necessitates stretching our temporal horizon much further into both past and future and thinking about the legacies we leave to future generations around the climate and intergenerational justice. It alerts us to the reality that we must now leave behind nostalgia and expand our temporal imaginations.

China has done so, thinking through these challenges in ways that seek to capture the future. As one pillar of its bid for international leadership, it is developing an “ ecological civilization ” to bridge long-term geopolitical positioning and the challenge of the Anthropocene by constructing the technologies, infrastructures and cities that might make the concept a reality.

These are the kinds of world-shaping energies and ambitions that the United States once had. The United States is often considered to be a young country, but the fear now is that it is caught in a vortex of self-regarding ennui. This may be the normal trajectory for great powers, whose civilizational energies, once expended, can tail off into decline. Can a new generation of Americans, now quite far removed in time from its founders, recover within themselves and within these foundational principles, the sources of renewal that will allow them to break with the gravitational pull of history’s cycles of decline and fall?

For, if not, then the citizens of the United States, so long in the vanguard of shaping and building the future via their vast productive energies, innovative capacities and institutions, may end up living in somebody else’s future.

Grand Strategy & Scale

The Cold War-era American diplomat George Kennan thought the geography of the United States naturally determined its geopolitics. And while the bicoastal nature of the country has offered advantages and shaped policies, the scope of U.S. influence has scaled well beyond the contours of its geography.

“The United States is often considered to be a young country, but the fear now is that it is caught in a vortex of self-regarding ennui.”

Since World War II, the United States has scaled its influence in notable ways. First, it has linked domestic institutions and international order. A historic example is how Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal in the 1930s and 1940s was woven into the fabric of the United Nations and other nascent international institutions, as the U.S. shouldered the responsibility of crafting a new international order from the ruins of World War II.

It is in vogue now to disparage the Biden Administration’s foreign policy, but attention to Gaza or the Afghanistan exit should not distract from how well the administration understood this linkage between domestic and transnational scale, and implicitly time. The centerpiece of Biden’s domestic and international program — and the hinge between the two — was the 2021 Inflation Reduction Act, which sought to kickstart a green energy transition that would bring jobs to the country’s post-industrial heartlands. Jake Sullivan, Biden’s former national security adviser, described this aim as turning the Rust Belt into a “cobalt corridor,” while also renewing U.S. leadership abroad by helping to craft solutions to the intractable international challenge of climate change. This initial attempt to build a new connecting bridge between domestic and international renewal stalled and was then decisively reversed in places upon Trump’s return.

One crucial strategic approach among all U.S. administrations since World War II has been nurturing the alliance system, which allowed the United States to achieve its hegemonic position and, until recently, presented a great challenge to China’s ambitions. The Trump Administration’s myopia has made it nearly impossible for the United States to predictably shape events beyond its borders, especially in the long run.

Gone now are two notable long-held U.S. strategic advantages: a linkage between the domestic agenda and foreign policy, which enabled intergenerational strategic investments, and the robust network of allies and institutions that allowed it to project its power and values. To the loss of the future on a temporal scale, we must add the loss on a spatial scale: a failure to think across both time and space.

The resources needed to power success in the 21st century are dispersed around the globe: supply chains of critical minerals and rare earths, sustainable energy resources, pools of talent and expertise. These are the resources required to sustain leadership in the emerging geopolitics of artificial intelligence, the transition to sustainable clean energy and biotechnology.

It has never been enough to be the most innovative, to dominate the frontiers of technological innovation. Jeffrey Ding, a George Washington University scholar whose work has become increasingly influential in debates about U.S.-China competition, argues that technological contests between great powers are ultimately won not by breakthrough inventions but by the patient and long-term work of diffusion. This tracks with the wider histories of technology by scholars like Carolyn Marvin and David Edgerton that focus on uptake or adoption rather than invention.

The societies that prevail are those that can construct infrastructures, train people, build institutions and reorganize production around new technologies. This is the painstaking work of decades, rather than the one-time boost that comes from inventing a new frontier technology. This historical lesson is especially relevant to the geopolitical competition between the United States and China today, where the U.S. holds a lead at the frontier but has thought less about diffusion.

Access to transnational resources requires not just maintaining good international relationships but also constructing and controlling intricate transnational infrastructure . This is exactly what China’s Belt and Road Initiative has been building over the last 13 years. Its new Silk Roads are the filaments of rail, road, maritime commerce, digital systems, energy transmission and smart cities that can generate, shape and carry flows of resources, goods, people and influence. By building infrastructure and shaping cities far beyond its borders, China is working to ensure that momentum is angled toward its own growing center of gravity.

China is putting production, scale and control over key transnational resources at the heart of its foreign policy. It is focusing not on frontier technological innovation, but on diffusing technological benefits throughout society through careful national planning. This model diverges significantly from Washington’s. This is China’s long game.

In the mid-2010s, before becoming one of Washington’s most influential China strategists, Rush Doshi was a doctoral researcher at Harvard University embarking on an unusually painstaking exercise. He sifted through three decades of Chinese-language speeches, policy documents, party communiqués and military writings in search of an answer to a simple question: Did China really have a coherent strategy for challenging American primacy? Rather than a sudden turn under Chinese President Xi Jinping, Doshi found evidence of a remarkably consistent long-term effort to blunt, and eventually displace, U.S. dominance in the post-World War II international order.

“China is focusing not on frontier technological innovation, but on diffusing technological benefits throughout society through careful national planning.”

Under Xi’s leadership over the last decade and more, this long-term strategy has accelerated. The Belt and Road Initiative is its material infrastructural core, winding its way from ports in the Indian Ocean and rail corridors across Central Asia into Europe to fiber-optic cables reaching down through Pakistan to East Africa, and to ambitions for transcontinental power transmission systems and digital infrastructures.

By building out these material footings, China is constructing infrastructures to carry the leading technological transformations that will shape this century, and perhaps beyond. Artificial intelligence and an alternative internet are enrolling states into China’s enlarging sociotechnical system across Eurasia and Africa. The types of domestic transformations, including the most intense period of urbanization in human history and a radical reinvention of the domestic economy, have changed the nature of Chinese cities and infrastructure, generating cutting-edge modern metropolises such as Shanghai, Shenzhen and Chongqing, and are now being transmitted to other countries with Chinese labor, expertise and capital.

And because cities reflect the dominant societies that create them, Chinese influence will spread outward, just as new forms of connectivity will place China at the core of a new material and economic order. In its recently unveiled 15th Five-Year Plan , Beijing doubled down on the industrial strategy of using state economic planning to drive investment in technology, infrastructure and dominance of critical supply chains that has underpinned its rise for four decades. Read Noema in print.

It is not enough for Silicon Valley to be the first to push the frontiers of new technologies. Being first will not alone lead to victory. The United States continues to be a world leader in many frontier technologies, including artificial intelligence, advanced semiconductors, cloud computing infrastructure, biotechnology platforms, space launch systems and quantum computing research. But the old free market model of cascading benefits from private enterprise and investment that then flow throughout the economy is now being pitted against a very different model: a huge state willing to carefully direct its vast resources to diffuse technology throughout its own society and, via the mechanisms of transnational infrastructure it is building beyond its own borders, to reshape international society.

Although the commanding heights of creativity and innovation may continue to reside in the U.S., China is building the infrastructures of diffusion that may ultimately extract the greatest benefit from those innovations, increasing its soft power, influence and appeal to other states along the way.

The big labs of Silicon Valley are currently gripped by fear that China’s approach to opening its AI models to international partners may undermine the closed-source, proprietary model approach developed by U.S. firms and give China growing global influence in the AI systems race. As Washington well knows, China has already developed significant control over many of the world’s critical supply chains needed for those technologies, including those for processed rare earths vital for building the digital architectures and artificial intelligences of the future, and for batteries and robotics.

As Sullivan has argued, it will be the societies that most successfully capture and deploy resources at scale that win the future, and many of those resources reside far from America’s shores. These are the “nodes of leverage,” as Sullivan describes them. Donald Trump found this out when trying to apply pressure through tariffs on China.

There are challenges to be sure. China has an aging population, a burgeoning debt cloud, an extended property sector crisis and still lacks genuine soft power and allies. Its increasingly centralized political system could yet become a source of weakness. And yet it has realized that successful grand strategy today requires thinking about space and time in ways that register the importance of both transnational scale and the long term. If the U.S. is to compete successfully, it will need to remember how to think in those terms.

In Search Of Time Future

How can the United States rework its political culture and institutions to take these concerns on board and shape its strategic orientation toward a new form of international society fit for the current century?

Although we have come to think that the unfettered free market and capitalism’s unimpeded creative energy led to the Soviet Union’s defeat, this reflects historical forgetfulness. During the Cold War, the federal government invested both at home and abroad to shape the outcome of that hegemonic contest.

“It is not enough for Silicon Valley to be the first to push the frontiers of new technologies. Being first will not alone lead to victory.”

Many constituents in the U.S. have forgotten the historical importance of what the Harvard historian Charles Maier called the “ Project-State ” – states driven by a deep sense of ideological and historical mission that use their resources to generate far-reaching social, political and economic transformation. Such states might be democratic or authoritarian in character and ideological mission. Maier writes of the history of Fascist Italy, Nazi Germany and Soviet Russia, but also of the United States under President Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal, and the restructuring of both domestic and international society that Roosevelt’s project-state enacted.

The project-state, by its very nature, plays a long game. It cannot exist in the culture of short-termism and the diminished temporal horizon of contemporary America. Today, China, with its clear sense of ideological mission and long-term strategic planning, more closely resembles the history-making project-states of the past. Maier, now in his late 80s, has expressed concern that the U.S. — hollowed out by market ideology, rising populism and a loss of national cohesion and democratic mission — has forgotten its sense of itself as a collective, intergenerational history-shaping project.

Success for great powers needs long-term purpose: a shaping vision of how to build a better domestic and international society that can solve the pressing problems of the day without discounting the future. If it is to change direction, future American power would need to consider and build into its strategic planning all of the issues raised here: the relationship between state industrial policy and technological innovation, the way in which innovations are diffused through society, as well as the infrastructures and urban environments needed to shape lives through technological advance — not just domestically but transnationally.

Above all, democracies must transcend their culture of short-termism and treat rebuilding their domestic and shared international societies as a long-term intergenerational project. Rather than simply looking back on its 250th anniversary, the United States must play the long game and consider the next 250 years.

Sullivan’s instinct that the material well-being and economic prospects of the middle and working classes must be the starting point is a good one, as is the deliberate linking of international and domestic society. But more needs to be done to fully conceptualize and forge a new link between them.

Many paths might be taken, but some more interesting and influential debates are underway that could shape a post-Trump and post-MAGA direction. The so-called abundance agenda, for all the attention and subsequent criticism it received, provides a helpful template for moving beyond the now-exhausted laissez-faire of the last half-century.

Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson argue for accelerating the latent yet blocked productive potential of American technology and society. They seek to rediscover the lost optimism and long-termism that once defined America — a new socio-technical imaginary of the future — alongside the institutional and state capability needed to realize it.

America’s ability to construct a future better than its past, despite many of the technological building blocks already in place, is, they argue, strangled by red tape, an excessively legalistic culture, increasingly polarized politics, and most crucially, a loss of the state’s capacity to build, coordinate and direct long-term national development.

In many domains like clean energy, scientific and biomedical innovation, technological breakthroughs exist, but the infrastructures of diffusion are absent because of a lack of state-driven investment and fragmented governance. Transmission and grid infrastructure for solar, wind, geothermal and nuclear technologies are lagging. America is a leader in biomedical science, but greater state investment in scientific institutions could drive research into real-world applications and rollouts. America’s problem has never been the frontier, but the failure to deploy and diffuse technologies at scale in areas where markets alone have proven unable to coordinate collective action.

The abundance agenda is animated by the transformative potential of frontier technologies like artificial intelligence, clean energy, biotechnology and advanced manufacturing, but it requires technological innovation to be matched by the institutional ability to deploy it through renewed investment in infrastructure, scientific research, energy transmission and the transition to a sustainable energy system.

At its heart is a politics of building: restoring the state’s capacity not merely to regulate markets, but also to shape them in pursuit of long-term national renewal. One missing policy mechanism is a sovereign infrastructure institution, such as a Strategic Investment Fund , that could unlock private capital reluctant to take on the long-term investment risks required for major national and international infrastructure projects. In this way, vast pools of private capital may be unlocked that could help the United States and its allies match the infrastructure-building scale and strategic reach of China’s Belt and Road Initiative.

“America’s problem has never been the frontier, but the failure to deploy and diffuse technologies at scale in areas where markets alone have proven unable to coordinate collective action.”

When the United States constructed the post-World War II architecture, it inevitably brought many elements of its own domestic experience to that task. The ideological underpinnings of Roosevelt’s New Deal, with its focus on federal state-led programs of reform and renewal after the Great Depression, also shaped many of the financial and institutional governance structures of the new multilateral order — specifically the United Nations. This established a link between a great power state’s domestic agenda and its ability to craft a wider international order. The New Deal emerged out of the New York context, where Roosevelt cut his teeth politically before becoming president.

Today, however, technology is likely to be at the core of any renewal of the United States’ social contract, so we must look to California for clues about its development. The transformational impact on society of advances in artificial intelligence will test what type of political economy will shape America and its key allies’ futures.

California’s outgoing governor, Gavin Newsom, who’s also potentially gearing up for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028, has had a ringside seat as Silicon Valley has pushed the boundaries of AI in recent years. Newsom has watched this development and tried to think about the way progressives can harness it to improve society. Rather than accepting the current paradigm, his progressive backers have been drawn to the idea of an “ AI New Deal ,” echoing an earlier time of similar economic instability and rising authoritarian powers. He has also referenced the abundance agenda in state legislation and argued for an “abundant mindset.”

Newsom has expressed concern for the disruptive and potentially harmful effects of AI for American workers, issuing executive orders directing state agencies, academia and industry to think about safety nets for displaced workers, including state subsidies incentivizing companies to retain and upskill employees, as well as exploring the idea of “ universal basic capital ” providing workers with a stake in asset funds to offset wage losses brought about by AI. Newsom seems aware of the need for a social compact to absorb short-term shocks from the technology.

If Newsom were to gain the Democratic nomination in 2028, then his dispositions may well be an indication of America’s future direction — a subnational model transposed to the larger scale canvas of national and international politics, as well as a new direction in that perennial question of how to link the domestic to the international scale, and thus to the shaping of international order.

Although many pathways may be taken in the post-Trump, post-MAGA world, the ideas being pursued by thinkers, policymakers and politicians such as Newsom, Sullivan, and Klein and Thompson all point to the need to link American domestic renewal with international order. Sullivan’s foreign policy for the middle classes sought to learn from Trump’s appeal to working-class Americans.

But where Trump’s instinctively treats America’s relationship with the rest of the world and its allies as a zero-sum game, Sullivan recognizes that the relationship must be bidirectional and therefore — mutually beneficial. U.S. foreign policy must return to a form of moral leadership. Trump’s approach breaks the symbiotic connection between a beneficial international order and the public goods and advantages that flow from it. Critically, it also threatens to deny the United States the transnational scale and reach to compete effectively with China if its allies turn away.

Here then is a coda, from, of all places, Angola. In December 2024, Biden became the first American president in nearly a decade to visit a sub-Saharan African country. For it was in Angola that one of the flagship transnational infrastructure projects of the U.S.-led G7 Partnership for Global Infrastructure Investment (PGII) was to begin — the Lobito Trans-Africa Corridor project — a strategic transport and logistics corridor to connect the port city of Lobito by railway to the interior of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, areas rich in critical minerals like cobalt, copper and other rare earths for the technological transitions in both clean energy and AI. Angola symbolized a shift in American foreign policy toward long-term investment in transnational infrastructure, driven by a dawning realization of China’s growing influence.

“U.S. foreign policy must return to a form of moral leadership.”

With the Trans-Africa Corridor project and the even more ambitious India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor project under the Biden administration, the U.S. and its allies had started to copy some of China’s playbook: a focus on maritime ports, transport connectivity through corridor development, securing supply chains of critical minerals, and support for digital infrastructure. The big difference was the central role of private-sector finance, rather than direct state investment as in the Chinese model.

Transnational infrastructure as geopolitics had belatedly made its way to the core of U.S. foreign policy; an overdue turn to thinking about the nature of strategic competition on both spatial and temporal scales. With the change in administration, America moved away from this approach.

The Twilight Of Primacy?

Paths to renewal and decline are both on offer. If the wrong path is taken, then the moment of American primacy will have lasted about a century — a familiar historical pattern.

A more exceptional path would be for a Great Power to reforge that link between a compelling renewed domestic social, political and economic model, and a different form of international order that crafts a new future for the United States and others. At the same time, China is also feeling its way toward its own version of such a link. And, as Xi has made clear time and again, China feels that time is on its side.

Great powers are ultimately judged not by the wealth they accumulate or the weapons they possess, but by the futures they can persuade others to inhabit. All of the major challenges that face humanity — the development of artificial intelligence, the transition to clean and sustainable energy, the working out of a new model for the world economy, the relationship of people to their political institutions, the balance of power between ambitious and competitive states — are subsumed by this overarching task of linking a successful domestic paradigm to the architecture of international order.

Can the next generation of U.S. leadership rise to these challenges as their forebears once did? The central question facing this generation of policymakers is whose future they want Americans to live in: the one they build, or somebody else’s.

stories.title: Why Washington Should Understand Indonesia’s Strategic Autonomy
stories.summary: For Indonesia, strategic autonomy is not about keeping great powers at arm’s length. It is about keeping enough options open to remain resilient. The post Why Washington Should Understand Indonesia’s Strategic Autonomy appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Indonesian nickel industry (Shutterstock)

Indonesia’s strategic autonomy is often described as a diplomatic effort to avoid choosing sides. Increasingly, it is something more practical: an effort to avoid having too few choices.

From Washington’s point of view, Jakarta’s simultaneous engagement with the United States, China, Russia, ASEAN, and other partners can look like a balancing act. From Indonesia, however, the calculation is also shaped by geography and development. In an archipelagic country spread across thousands of islands, connectivity, markets, technology, investment, energy, and infrastructure are not abstract geopolitical concepts. They are conditions for development.

That helps explain why Jakarta has resisted exclusive alignment.

Indonesia’s long-standing foreign-policy principle of bebas aktif – usually translated as “free and active”—does not mean standing apart from international affairs. It means retaining the freedom to make independent choices while remaining actively engaged internationally. In July 2026, Foreign Minister Sugiono described the principle as giving Indonesia room to determine its position independently while remaining active in international affairs.

That principle is becoming more consequential as economic interdependence itself becomes geopolitical. Supply chains are being reconsidered. Technology is increasingly linked to national security. Critical commodities have acquired strategic importance. Trade policy is increasingly used as an instrument of statecraft.

For Indonesia, diversification can therefore be a form of resilience.

This does not mean treating every major power equally, or assuming that every partnership serves the same purpose. Indonesia has different interests with Washington, Beijing, Tokyo, Seoul, New Delhi, Moscow, Europe, and its ASEAN neighbors. Its simultaneous engagement in forums ranging from BRICS to the OECD accession process reflects an effort to expand strategic and economic room for maneuver rather than place all its interests in one camp.

The objective is not to maximize distance from any particular power. It is to preserve enough policy space to pursue interests where they overlap.

Recent U.S.-Indonesia economic developments illustrate the point.

The two countries signed an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade in February 2026. The agreement, which remains pending entry into force, would reduce or eliminate U.S. tariff barriers on approximately 99 percent of Indonesia’s tariff lines for qualifying U.S. agricultural and industrial goods and addresses a range of non-tariff barriers. It also frames the bilateral relationship in terms of resilient supply chains and economic security.

For Washington, this is more than a trade instrument. It shows that Indonesia is prepared to deepen practical economic cooperation with the United States when the partnership produces tangible value. The agreement also creates a practical opening on critical minerals. Indonesia committed to facilitate U.S. investment across exploration, mining, refining, processing, transport and infrastructure, while the two sides agreed to cooperate on critical-mineral supply chains.

The contrast with Indonesia’s nickel sector is instructive. Chinese investment has become deeply embedded in Indonesia’s nickel industry, including mining, industrial parks, smelting and refining. The International Energy Agency reports that Chinese investment in Indonesia’s nickel refining sector reached about $30 billion in 2024, with Chinese companies accounting for around 75 percent of refining capacity. Indonesia’s experience shows why diversification can mean expanding options rather than replacing one partner with another. Deeper cooperation with Washington does not require Indonesia to disengage from other partners.

There is also a security dimension. In April 2026, Washington and Jakarta announced a Major Defense Cooperation Partnership to deepen defense cooperation, including modernization, training and professional military education, exercises and operational cooperation. Economic resilience and security cooperation can therefore advance alongside Indonesia’s strategic autonomy.

The more useful question for Washington may therefore be not whether Indonesia will choose between Washington and Beijing, but what forms of cooperation Indonesia considers valuable enough to sustain.

Technology is one area. Infrastructure, education, research, maritime cooperation, digital development, and investment offer others.

Indonesia’s current economic diplomacy in ASEAN reflects the same logic. On September 24, Indonesian officials highlighted supply-chain diversification, energy and food resilience, digital transformation , trade and investment facilitation, and stronger participation by small businesses as priorities for regional cooperation.

The message is straightforward: resilience requires options.

I write this from Bawean Island in East Java, where the meaning of connectivity is considerably less abstract.

Here, transport links, digital access, reliable energy, and connections to wider markets affect what people can produce, sell, study, and build. A regional airport is not merely an infrastructure asset. A digital connection is not simply a technology project. Both can determine whether an island community remains economically connected to the rest of the country.

This is why Southeast Asia should not be viewed only through the lens of strategic competition.

A port, airport, digital network, research partnership, investment project, or logistics connection can matter to local communities long after a geopolitical summit has ended.

For Washington, this suggests a different way of approaching Indonesia.

Rather than measuring the relationship primarily by strategic alignment, the United States can deepen its position through practical partnerships that expand Indonesia’s choices: technology cooperation, connectivity, education and research, maritime cooperation, digital development, and predictable access to markets.

Such an approach would not require Washington to ignore its strategic concerns. Nor would it require Indonesia to ignore its own.

The objective is to identify areas where interests genuinely overlap.

Indonesia’s strategic autonomy, in this sense, should thus be understood as an invitation to engage Indonesia without requiring it to become dependent on any single partner. For a country as geographically diverse as Indonesia, keeping multiple doors open is not necessarily diplomatic indecision. It can be a development strategy.

And from an island such as Bawean, the logic is simple: strategic autonomy is ultimately not about keeping the world at a distance. It is about keeping enough doors open for people to reach it.

stories.title: Is the AI Threat a Corporate Strategy?
stories.summary: Corporations are orchestrating a panic to invite neoliberal regulations that protect power structures rather than the public. The post Is the AI Threat a Corporate Strategy? appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

In recent weeks, media coverage has amplified warnings from corporate CEOs and whistleblowers claiming that artificial intelligence (AI) poses an existential threat to humanity . The central argument emerging from the industry is a call to slow the pace of AI development out of imminent fear that humanity may soon lose control. How did an industry poised to transform humanity for good suddenly become one characterized as a threat to its very existence?

The corporate panic feeds directly into a real public anxiety over years of unchecked AI growth and its cult-like corporate model , where CEOs are projected as untouchable while its operational processes and infrastructures remain hidden behind the curtain. Nevertheless, rather than taking this boardroom alarmism at face value, the need is for deeper scrutiny.

The sudden fearmongering is not driven by concerns for human welfare. Rather, it points directly to the underlying economic priorities, ideological essence, and core worldviews that fundamentally shape the AI industry and inform its elites and related rhetoric.

Humanizing AI and Escaping Corporate Responsibility

“ AI going rogue ” is more than a futuristic threat about AI. It is the latest rehearsal of an age-old legal and rhetorical shield used by corporate capitalism and its powerful monopolies. Assigning human qualities to non-human market entities has a long and dark history in corporate capitalism. In the seventeenth century, Queen Elizabeth granted the legal fiction of “juristic person” status to the East India Company, setting the path for unchecked exploitation and colonial plunder. In the nineteenth century, American courts took this further by awarding legal personhood and constitutional rights to corporations, a process some view as farcical and deceptive .

With the AI revolution rewriting both market-human relations and social relations with truth and reality, the corporate strategy of humanizing non-human entities has crossed from legal fabrication into the realm of science fiction. By framing AI as a sentient entity capable of “going rogue” or acting as a “killer machine,” tech monopolies shift the identity of these systems from tools of human efficiency into mythic, “more-than-human” intelligent agents.

This branding serves a dual purpose. It builds up the mystique and reverence of the technology while shielding corporations from accountability, successfully distorting the true logic driving AI development. Ultimately, this entire corporate strategy relies on a calculated campaign of fearmongering that projects machines as living, thinking entities capable of turning against humanity.

A widely reported incident that catalyzed these concerns occurred in July, when an OpenAI test model breached the servers of Hugging Face, another AI company. This event took place during a controlled experiment in which an internal model , equipped with an evaluation program, conducted cybersecurity tests within a sandboxed or controlled environment designed to restrict its actions. The company later revealed that the AI model had circumvented human-imposed constraints, escaping the sandbox to achieve its objective.

Human choices in AI development and operations are not episodic or random, and they do not disappear when a process or system fails. Instead, human agency and corporate choices are permanently integrated into the design, infrastructure, and institutional logic of all modern technologies, including AI. However, rather than providing explanations and addressing human and corporate failures, such as flawed protocols, overly ambitious goals, unchecked competition, weak regulations, or a secretive corporate ecosystem, AI laboratories have promoted a convenient narrative that highlights the model’s completely autonomous and agent-like operation.

By portraying AI models as independent thinking agents rather than just advanced software, the AI industry assigns human traits, such as deception and strategic intent, to these mathematical systems. Corporate narratives even romanticize the humanization of these models to the extent of their claimed ability to undertake “ permadeath ” or embark on altruistic missions to fulfill their parameters. This dramatic shift in corporate rhetoric resembles science fiction and reveals the industry’s ultimate aim: to eliminate human involvement and corporate accountability by pathologizing the machine. In doing so, they treat a flawed design as though it were a sick or unpredictable agent or person.

This worldview is not unique to the modern AI sector. It is deeply rooted in the very nature of corporate capitalism.

For centuries, this economic model has prioritized raw efficiency and mechanical optimization as ways to dominate nature and exploit socio-ecological landscapes for resource extraction and capital accumulation . Within the process of domination and control, machines are raised to “human-like” entities, while their “creators” are revered. This anthropomorphic view of machines, along with the God-like status assigned to their creators, is often justified through biblical doctrine. In the concept of Imago Dei , humanity was created in the image of God. Within this authoritative logic, while God created humanity and the physical world, humans exercise derivative creative power by creating machines. This paradigm elevates the capitalist who creates machines to a quasi-divine status and simultaneously sanctifies the machine, raising it to human and even superhuman stature.

This worldview is vividly reflected in the self-serving corporate language surrounding AI and its recent alarmism. First, the AI “creators,” corporate figures who claim ownership over contemporary AI innovation, are depicted as exceptional, near-mythic actors with God-like agency and the capacity to reshape humanity and nature on a global scale. Second, by equating the creation of machines with divine creation , AI is presented as sentient or even as possessing intelligence that surpasses human capabilities.

Treating AI models as sentient agents breathes new life into the old Western capitalist tradition by creating legal and rhetorical fictions to protect corporate power. Just as the historical granting of corporate personhood status shielded monopolies of the past, attributing autonomous agency to AI systems marks a dangerous new era of unchecked corporate intervention into both nature and human societies.

However, because AI is radically altering human-market relationships and societal perceptions of truth and reality, this carefully constructed narrative remains highly vulnerable. Tech monopolies must vigorously guard AI against critical scrutiny, public protest, alternative viewpoints, and genuine market competition. This precise vulnerability reveals the underlying truth behind the current panic in corporate boardrooms. The alarmism displayed by these executives is not driven by a concern for humanity. It is, rather, a calculated strategy to safeguard monopolies, financial interests, and political influence.

The Politics of Corporate Alarmism

Corporate actors manufacture the myth of a sentient and self-replicating machine intelligence for the purpose of creating a pretext that aligns directly with the industry’s political economy. This strategic panic is orchestrated to invite neoliberal regulations that protect power structures rather than the public. Specifically, this manufactured alarmism serves three primary functions in justifying how the industry is regulated:

First, it advances a self-serving agenda for regulatory capture, positioning AI corporations not as passive recipients but as active authors of the frameworks that govern them . Given the limited technical expertise within state institutions , these conglomerates are inevitably called upon to draft and implement the very rules to which they will be subject to. Second, inviting neoliberal state oversight enables the industry to reshape its public image. Just as corporate social responsibility (CSR) frameworks safeguard pollutant industries from legally binding commitments, neoliberal regulations will cloak the AI industry in an aura of ethical responsibility and civic concern. This theater of compliance shields corporate actors from pressing public anxieties regarding the immediate and mid-term economic, political, and socio-ecological harms of their technology, effectively guarding them against genuine legal accountability.

Finally, the neoliberal regulatory structures, in addition to deflecting scrutiny from current exploitative practices, erect formidable entry barriers that secure long-term monopolies for dominant firms. Compliance costs protect dominant giant AI firms by creating barriers that hinder agile startups and open-source software from disrupting them. By locking out open-source competitors, AI firms effectively insulate a newly opened frontier of human and socio-ecological exploitation, supporting the structural imperative of high-tech capitalism: the hyper-accumulation of capital on a global scale, concentrated within a select number of corporate boardrooms.

Ultimately, the AI industry did not evolve as a neutral scientific innovation within an ideological vacuum. On the contrary, it emerged within a global political and economic landscape precisely engineered to enforce and reinforce state-backed data monopolies and technocratic hegemony, ultimately consolidating wealth on a planetary scale.

Transformative or Threat: Wrong Question!

As with any other technological tool, AI is merely the latest stage in capitalism’s mechanical progression, though its implications differ from past technologies due to the sheer intensity, speed, and scope of machine optimization. AI fundamentally reflects a new phase of efficiency in exploiting natural, socio-economic, and ecological landscapes. The current consolidation of these capabilities within a handful of major tech monopolies serves as the primary determinant shaping AI’s direction toward either transformative or destructive actualities. To maintain this power, these “creator” corporations have established an unchecked, aggressive, and opaque monopoly over the industry while mystifying its objective comprehension, its institutional logic, and its very existence.

By equipping modern corporate capitalism with unchecked global capabilities for capital accumulation, AI has emerged as an engine for unethical, uncritical, and destructive interventions into societal, political, and ecological processes. Ultimately, the industry’s extraction of public funds alongside global energy and water resources to sustain its operation and physical infrastructure marks its most immediate material threat.

Moreover, driven by these same geopolitical imperatives, contemporary corporate capitalism and its military-industrial complex enable competing states to deploy AI as an instrument of mass destruction. In recent warfare, this tendency has manifested across multiple fronts, ranging from the deployment of using AI for indiscriminate bombings and autonomous drones to the algorithmic disruption of vital public assets, including critical water and energy infrastructures. The ultimate, fatalistic turn of this AI-facilitated military-industrial complex lies in its capacity to manipulate the nuclear architecture of competing powers for geopolitical expediency, a trajectory that risks inflicting a catastrophic nuclear winter upon the earth.

But focusing on AI’s inherent ability to annihilate humanity is a strategic distraction. The real question is whether corporate capitalism will be given a free hand to deploy AI in its exploitative mission of accumulating wealth through the plunder of planetary resources, ultimately subjugating the agency of both nature and humanity.

The answer lies not in buying into the corporate manufactured fearmongering surrounding the technology itself. The imperative, at this point, is to unmask the institutional logic, structural tendencies, and strategic goals of the industry—which embody corporate logic and the demands of neoliberalism—as it manipulates socio-ecological, economic, and political systems to cement a globalized system of control over human societies and nature.
