Jeremy Clarkson: Farming this year was 'an absolute disaster'

Published 5 October 2026

Jeremy Clarkson has said it had been a "terrible" year for farming due to the hot weather, at a surprise appearance at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.

The former Top Gear presenter and star of Clarkson's Farm also said farmers were being "attacked" from every angle by rising costs, but he was optimistic about the future.

He was greeted by loud applause from the Tory faithful, but joked that "a lot of people have come dressed as seats, I notice, around the edges there".

In a question and answer session alongside land agent Charlie Ireland, he also criticised the economic conditions faced by business owners, asking: "Why would anybody set up a business in this country right now?"

Clarkson - who also hosts ITV's Who Wants to be a Millionaire - was introduced to the stage by the Conservative shadow environment secretary Victoria Atkins.

Asked what kind of year he had had on the farm, Clarkson said: "We worked really hard all year and we ended up with, I think I'm right in saying, three ounces of hen food.

"It was an absolute disaster on the farming side but, I mean, luckily we've got other projects going on now.

"But the farming is very, very difficult – very, very difficult at the moment."

He added: "I'm very fortunate that I do have other income streams and newspaper columns, but if you're an ordinary farmer, it's not just the weather.

"Remember, it's as Charlie was saying, the attacks come from everywhere – whether it's Iran or Ukraine or taxes or energy costs – whatever it might be, it's just relentless."

The TV presenter has long been a Conservative supporter and was involved in the campaign against the Labour government's inheritance tax plans for farmers .

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government would levy inheritance tax on family farms in the party's first budget.

But the plan was watered down last year following the farmers' campaign and pressure from some of Labour's rural MPs.

Responding to Clarkson's comments, a government source said: "We are working with farmers to strengthen domestic food production and make supply chains more resilient as we build a stronger and more profitable farming sector together."

Clarkson also joked about comments by Labour MP Jenny Riddell-Carpenter who said the Britain of country pubs and black Labradors was a "nostalgic" false memory.

He joked that he was a "socialist" because he drinks lager and has two fox red Labradors, after it was reported Riddell-Carpenter told a Labour conference fringe event she feared the far right deciding what the vision of rural areas is.

Riddell-Carpenter had said: "It'll be that warm ale, a black Labrador by your feet in a pub that doesn't exist, and with symbolism of fox hunting all around them. It'll be a very far-right nostalgic vision of Britain that we don't want to have, (that) never really existed."

O'Neill said she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them"

Published 5 October 2026

First Minister Michelle O'Neill has dismissed a call from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) to resign over her role in protests against the Drumcree parade.

The Sinn Féin vice-president was branded the "first minister of lawlessness" as unionists criticised the demonstrations on Garvaghy Road.

Police are investigating the unlawful protests which blocked an Orange Order march from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh.

Facing questions in the Stormont assembly, O'Neill said she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them".

She described the planned Orange march on 27 September as "unwanted, sectarian and triumphalist".

O'Neill was speaking on Monday in response to an urgent question on the Drumcree dispute tabled by DUP assembly member Phillip Brett.

O'Neill returns to Garvaghy Road as police investigate Sunday's 'unlawful protest' Published 6 days ago

Court of Appeal reserves judgement over Drumcree parade dispute Published 1 day ago

An uneasy peace – how a week of the Drumcree parade dispute has unfolded Published 3 days ago

Michelle O'Neill was speaking in response to an urgent question from DUP MLA Phillip Brett

He called on O'Neill to "drop the bravado" and claimed she had shown "utter contempt" for the ministerial pledge of office.

Brett continued: "If you have been found to breach the ministerial code or the law, will you do the decent thing for once and resign as first minister?"

The first minister responded: "Catch yourself on, would be where I would start with that one.

"I'm going to continue to turn up for the people of the Garvaghy Road.

"I'm proud to stand with them and I will continue to stand with them."

Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) assembly member Timothy Gaston accused O'Neill of being the "first minister of lawlessness" over her role in the street protests.

O'Neill replied: "I am the first minister of what is right."

She added that "we won't need to AI it" - a reference to a TUV councillor who posted online an AI image which exaggerated the size of a loyalist rally in Portadown.

DUP assembly member Jonathan Buckley questioned whether O'Neill would "accept and abide by the lawful decision of the courts" when appeal court judges make a ruling on the parade dispute.

Protesters along the Garvaghy Road, with the road blocked at a number of points on 27 September

The first minister said that "when the law is wrong I will stand firmly against it" and described the planned march as "morally wrong".

O'Neill later said "shame on you" to DUP assembly members over the party's handling of the Drumcree dispute.

"Your party has championed this," she said to DUP members on the opposite benches.

O'Neill flatly rejected a claim from Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows that many people now regarded the first minister as "completely morally bankrupt".

Earlier, Stormont Speaker Edwin Poots raised concerns over the first minister not attending the chamber last week to answer the tabled urgent question.

The DUP assembly member said O'Neill's absence last Monday was "discourteous" to the assembly and the public.

"Members know my views on ministers being accountable to this house on behalf of the people who put us all here," he said.

stories.title: Shadow chancellor vows to cut at least one tax in every Tory budget
stories.summary: Shadow ministers unveiled a series of policies on day two of the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 October 2026

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said he hopes to scrap at least one tax every budget if the Conservatives return to power, with the so-called "mansion tax" in his sights.

Speaking at the party's conference in Birmingham, Griffith said "lower, simpler and fairer taxes" would be his "personal north star" although he noted his ambition for cuts would take place "only when we can afford to do so".

He also said he would scrap the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), which takes effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m.

Labour said the Tories "completely failed at every turn" to grow the economy during their 14 years in power.

Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again.

The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government between 2010 and 2024.

Speaking on the main stage, Griffith said: "No country in history has ever taxed its way to prosperity, so we will cut taxes, but only when we can afford to do so, and always saying clearly how we will fund that within our golden economic rule."

The party's "golden economic rule" involves at least half of all savings identified going towards "deficit reduction, with the other half going to tax cuts and pro-growth measures".

Griffith likened his approach to that of former Tory Chancellor Nigel Lawson, adding: "It's my ambition to scrap at least one tax every budget. What would we prioritise? There's a lot.

"Tax cuts that help growth, tax cuts that improve incentives to work, tax cuts that make life simpler and fairer."

The Extended Packaging Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires firms to cover the cost of collecting, recycling and disposing of packaging it produces, would be scrapped by the Conservatives.

Griffith sought to signal a different approach under Kemi Badenoch's leadership, telling members that the EPR was the "sort of thing the old Conservative Party went along with".

He also said Labour plans a "vindicative raid on family homes" in the form of the HVCTS, also dubbed the "mansion tax", which he would seek to scrap.

The shadow chancellor said: "It's an anti-growth tax that will distort the housing market and remove the incentive to make home improvements."

Ahead of his speech, Griffith was pressed on BBC Breakfast on whether he would keep the pensions triple lock, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham has proposed changing.

Griffith said: "We are going to keep it."

In 2021, then-backbencher Griffith wrote an article saying that the state pension triple lock was "unfair" as pensioners could "gain from the misfortune of others".

Senior Conservatives including former chancellor Jeremy Hunt and shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat have individually suggested the current triple lock is unsustainable.

Properties worth more than £2m in England face mansion tax Published 3 December 2025

Tories committed to pension triple lock, deputy leader says Published 5 days ago

Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow Published 27 September

During a series of speeches on Monday, Griffith and other shadow ministers also announced further details on the policies they believe will help free up businesses and grow the economy.

The proposals included ditching environmental and energy efficiency regulations, such as the future homes standard.

Griffith said the next Conservative government would support a third runway at Heathrow Airport. Plans for expansion were scrapped by the Tory-led coalition government in 2010.

The Conservatives also want to implement a single levy for developers in place of section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy, which fund projects in the community when building plans are progressed.

The party has been critical of the roles of Natural England and the Environment Agency in relation to house building and flood prevention work respectively, and wants to abolish both. Their functions would be looked after by the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).

Prospect general secretary Mike Clancy, whose union represents members in Natural England and the Environment Agency, said: "Conservative budget cuts have left these regulators struggling to perform their vital functions with 'lack of resources' the most common reason for planning delays.

"The solution is to restore their funding to adequate levels, not scrap vital safeguards."

'Fantasy-land' pledges

Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the Conservatives have "cemented their position as a pointless anti-growth, anti-business party" by rejecting closer ties with Europe.

She added: "No-one can take anything the Conservatives say on the economy seriously given their litany of fantasy-land financial pledges."

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories had 14 years in government to grow our economy and help people get on the housing ladder, but they completely failed at every turn."

Chancellor John Healey last week said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space".

Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick accused the Conservatives of "once again copying our policies".

He added the Tories were unable to match Reform's pledge to raise the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 .

Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said scrapping rules that "secure affordable homes and vital community infrastructure is not a plan for growth".

She added: "It is a gift to developers, leaving communities to pick up the bill for new housing while handing ordinary people higher costs and fewer protections."

stories.title: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws bombers
stories.summary: US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed on Sunday, following an incident near the base last week.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford

Published 5 October 2026

Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe, after the US withdrew all of its bombers from the military base.

The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.

US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed, which follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.

A No 10 spokesperson said he would not comment on "foreign nations' military operations", but said the base was safe, and pointed to US President Donald Trump's comments last week, where he "praised our police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.

Peace for villagers as US bombers leave UK airbase Published 1 day ago

What makes RAF Fairford one of the UK's most important military sites? Published 7 days ago

He added that Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had said last week, "we have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world".

Speaking on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.

He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."

Rubio said the US still has full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities have been very cooperative since the incident.

US Vice President JD Vance later said the bombers were moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington feels Iran is doing what it has "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".

RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - is at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.

Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.

Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.

The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.

Earlier on Monday, the New York Times reported US commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford according to two US officials.

The newspaper wrote that the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours.

Ezra Cohen, who served as a defence official under Trump's first administration, called the US' decision "prudent".

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "These are very, very unique platforms that aren't being produced anymore, and we have a limited number of them. The B-1 bomber is a strategic asset, and we're going to take steps to protect it from all sorts of threats."

It is technically possible for the US to conduct precision strikes directly from the US without a UK base - like in Operation Midnight Hammer last year .

But the removal of the bombers from RAF Fairford will see the US lose a foothold for the country outside continental Europe.

Liberal Democrat defence spokesperson James MacCleary called the US' decision to withdraw its bombers "deeply concerning" and called for the government to set out a plan to ensure the country's military bases are "fit for purpose".

Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

Residents living close to RAF Fairford told the BBC of their relief at the departure of bombers from the airbase, with one local saying she was "thrilled," citing the noise and feeling "increasingly vulnerable" in recent weeks.

Another villager, who said he has seen bombs being loaded aboard aircraft from his back garden, said he knew something was happening when he saw planes leaving "one, after another, after another" on Sunday.

stories.title: Would the Conservatives' plan make new houses £50,000 cheaper?
stories.summary: BBC Verify looks into the shadow chancellor's plan to cut some building regulations to reduce construction costs.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 October 2026

Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has said his party, if it was returned to power, would take £50,000 off the cost of building a new home in England and Wales by cutting back on regulations.

The £50,000 figure claimed by Griffith reflects estimates by the housebuilding industry of the costs of new regulations and taxes.

However, construction and housing experts warn that some of the savings could ultimately lead to higher government spending on schools, roads, and affordable housing.

And some analysts also warn the Conservative plans to scrap environmental regulations could potentially push up household energy bills in future.

Where does the £50,000 figure come from?

The Conservatives argue a number of regulations are adding to the cost of constructing and delivering new private homes.

These include:

The Community Infrastructure Levy - a charge on certain new developments in England and Wales which councils can use to fund local infrastructure such as roads, schools and play areas

The Future Homes Standard which requires new-build homes in England to meet higher energy-efficiency standards and use low-carbon heating such as heat pumps rather than gas boilers

Section 106 which can require developers to provide a proportion of social or affordable housing in England as part of a new development.

The Tories say they will scrap or reform these and other regulations, saying: "All in all, we will cut the cost of delivering and therefore buying a new home by up to £50,000."

BBC Verify has asked the Conservatives for a full breakdown of their figure.

What does the construction industry say?

The Home Builders Federation (HBF) has estimated that new regulations, taxes and inflation - since 2020 - have increased the cost of building an individual new home in England and Wales by £76,000.

It says this represents around 20% of the value of an average new home.

Of this total, it estimates:

£985 comes from Section 106

£10,200 comes from the Future Homes Standard

£12,700 in environmental protection measures such as "nutrient neutrality" and "biodiversity net gain"

Excluding a £37,000 increase in the costs of material and labour, the HBF estimates that regulations and taxes have added around £42,000 to the cost of building a new home.

The Conservatives' estimate is slightly higher than the HBF's figure. The HBF also includes nearly £8,000 to reflect changes in building regulations. The Conservatives have not said they would find savings by scrapping all of those.

The party's plan also assumes the savings they have highlighted would be passed on to buyers rather than raising house builders' profits.

Could these savings be achieved?

Noble Francis of trade body the Construction Products Association (CPA) told BBC Verify that new costs imposed on builders through regulations and taxes in recent years - including the time firms spend navigating the regulatory system - are a serious constraint on residential construction rates.

The Labour government is well off track in terms of meeting its target of building 1.5 million net additional dwellings in England over the course of this parliament - which requires an annual building rate of around 300,000 homes per year.

In the year to June only around 203,000 were built, according to official estimates.

However, Francis also said: "It's easy for any party not in government to just claim they will get rid of red tape and cut costs but both the Conservatives and Labour have been in power in the last five years and have added extra costs to house building."

The Future Homes Standard, for instance, was first proposed in 2019 when Conservative Prime Minister Boris Johnson was in power.

Other analysts point out that the upfront construction cost savings from the plan could potentially lead to higher government spending in the future.

Housing expert Anna Clarke said: "Cutting the costs of house building by £50,000 would be really helpful in getting much-needed new homes built.

"But if you don't get developers to pay for new schools and infrastructure you need to pay for them some other way."

And some analysts argue that updated environmental building standards, such as requiring heat pumps rather than gas boilers in new homes, are forecast to save households money in the long-term by reducing their domestic energy bills.

Dr Richard Lowes of clean energy advocates the Regulatory Assistance Project told BBC Verify: "If the energy bill implications are not carefully considered, households may be lumbered with very high bills for decades.

"The lowest running costs can typically be achieved with heat pumps paired with solar and batteries."

Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett and Daniel Wainwright

stories.title: Ex-Manchester leader defends deals with Man City owners
stories.summary: Veteran former council leader Sir Richard Leese says the relationship has been beneficial to the city.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sir Richard Leese was leader of Manchester City Council for 25 years before he stepped down in 2021

Published 5 October 2026

The former leader of Manchester City Council has defended the council's relationship with the owners of Manchester City amid questions over land deals.

Sir Richard Leese, who was head of the council for 25 years until 2021 and is also honorary president of the club, said a decade-old deal with Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) was "good for the city".

The partnership between the authority and the company owned by Sheik Mansour bin zayed Al Nahyan has come under renewed scrutiny since City was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations with "sham" commercial contracts .

The club has denied any wrongdoing is appealing against the charges.

The council entered into a partnership with ADUG in 2014 when they formed a joint venture called Manchester Life.

It planned to invest more than £1bn over the next decade and develop thousands of homes in the Ancoats and New Islington areas, on the edge of the city centre close to the club's Etihad stadium.

But in 2022, a report by the University of Sheffield, called Manchester Offshored, raised questions about the wider public value of the schemes, and a lack of transparency around their finances.

It highlighted the absence of any affordable housing in the projects, and that the joint venture companies were ultimately owned by ADUG through firms registered offshore.

Abu Dhabi United Group are majority shareholders in City Football Group - which owns Manchester City FC

A deal struck in 2015 saw ADUG effectively given the first pick of land in Ancoats and New Islington. The University of Sheffield report argued that land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates".

Sir Richard said the 2015 deal was "brokered by the UK government with the UAE government".

"It was a time when development in Manchester had stopped," he said.

"We were still suffering from the 2008 crash, from the recession that followed that.

"There was criticism at the time though - and there still is now - that the land was given away too cheaply by the city council.

"The point is, the investment from Abu Dhabi is what created the value.

"That deal allowed development to be kick-started - particularly in the Ancoats area.

"All of this was documented and went through reports that went through the council's due processes.

"I think it has been demonstrated that the deal was a good deal and a good deal for Manchester."

'Real credibility'

Abu Dhabi's investment in Manchester City started in 2008, when City Football Group – majority-owned by ADUG - bought the club in a £200m deal.

With significant investment from its new owners, the club went on to win its first trophy in 36 years with an FA Cup win in 2011 and a dramatic Premier League title followed the next year.

The club went on to win the league seven more times between 2013 and 2024.

But the Premier League began investigating the club's financial dealings in 2018, and City was charged in 2023.

Last week, it was announced the club had been found guilty of 115 charges, including some around a so-called disguised funding scheme, which was said to have seen the club's owners topping up sponsorship and commercial deals with their own funding running to more than £800m.

Andy Burnham has said Manchester City's owners had been a "huge partner" in Manchester

When asked last week about potential fallout from the City charges, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was metropolitan mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 to 2026, said he would be "really concerned" if the owners were to pull out of the club.

He added: "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."

Since then, it has been reported that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) may halt UK-wide investment schemes worth billions of pounds as a result of the Premier League ruling.

Sir Richard said he hoped that Manchester did not lose UEA investment, adding: "I think certainly Abu Dhabi will be thinking that they have been very badly treated given the contribution that they have made - not just to Manchester but to English football as well."

He added: "I would be concerned if they did stop investing. I don't think they'd give us up."

Sir Richard told BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier that "the investment in Manchester from Abu Dhabi has been very significant".

Stressing he was not speaking on behalf of the club, he pointed to the investment in City, its training complex and the City Football Group headquarters.

He added: "I think for the city, one thing about working with Abu Dhabi is everything that they promised they have delivered.

"So they have real credibility in the city. That's something we'd want to maintain.

"I don't think any other football club has got anywhere near the sort of contribution that they have made to their local community.

"What has been created in Manchester City is a phenomenon really and that has to be maintained in some way whatever the final outcome of the allegations against them."

'Achieved'

Manchester City Council also defended the benefits of the partnership with Manchester Life as a "platform for future development".

"The claim that working in partnership with Manchester City's owners has not been a good deal for the council or the city has been debunked repeatedly," the authority said.

"Claims that some land was sold too cheaply to Manchester Life ignore the fact that there was zero market interest at the time of the sale, that the land is worth more now precisely because of Manchester Life's investment and the significant financial return the council is receiving through profit-sharing arrangements.

"Manchester Life was always envisaged as a platform for further investment. Its success should be measured in what it has delivered directly and what it has unlocked.

"The partnership was set up to deliver significant housing development, create an investor confidence and a platform for other developers to come into the market and invest in Manchester - which it has achieved."

Published 5 October 2026

It is not exactly typical for a British party conference, let alone that of one of the smaller parties, to elicit international condemnation.

Yet that is the position the Green Party of England and Wales is in today after Israel's foreign ministry said it was banning their leader, Zack Polanski, from entering the country.

The cause was the motion proposed by party members and adopted by the conference on Sunday, declaring Zionism, which is the belief in the right to a Jewish homeland, to be racism.

The Green motion describes Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state", and supports instead a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

It's hardly likely that Polanski or indeed many Greens are going to be much troubled by Israel's condemnation of the motion. One major factor in the Greens' electoral gains over the past year or so, a hugely successful period for the party, has been their clear and vocal condemnation of Israel's war in Gaza and actions in the region more generally.

What may be more troubling for the Greens institutionally is what this episode reveals about some of the dynamics in the party.

Many Greens are proud of the party's internal democracy: this motion was proposed by and voted on by party members. Yet that has resulted in the scenario of leading Green elected politicians facing scrutiny over party policy which the vast majority of them opposed.

Polanski, who is not an MP, wanted changes to the motion which were rejected by the conference, and ultimately did not participate in the debate or vote. Of the Greens' five MPs, four opposed the motion.

The most vocal of them was Adrian Ramsay, the MP for Waveney Valley, who was a Green co-leader for four years until September last year when he and his running mate were defeated by Polanski by a vast margin.

Polanski banned from Israel after party's motion declaring 'Zionism is racism' Published 1 day ago

Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion Published 1 day ago

So an element of this is the changing nature of the Greens' activist base under Polanski's leadership, moving away from an environmental focus to a more general left-populist politics, incorporating a large element of 'anti-imperialist' foreign policy.

Yet this may not be the last issue where that results in a public dispute between the membership and their MPs, four of whom were elected at the last general election under different leadership.

And it is striking that, though Polanski's election as leader was a clear symbol of that shift in the Greens' approach, he did not back this motion. So this could presage tensions too between Polanski and the party membership, some of whom will have been inspired to join the Greens by his leadership.

In practical terms, the Green MPs will be able to continue espousing a different position in parliament to the party's new policy.

The Greens do not have a whipping system, meaning that MPs are free to vote as they wish. This is also true of their councillors, including in the almost 40 councils where the Greens are in power after the May local elections.

It will be interesting to see whether as a result of these tensions there is a push either to constrain the ability of the party conference to make policy, or in the other direction - to constrain the ability of elected representatives to defy party policy.

Electoral reform

Separately, this motion may present a political headache down the line for Andy Burnham.

In his Labour conference speech last week, the prime minister said he was forming a "national commission" on electoral reform, with a view to changing the system used for general elections in the long-term.

While Burnham did not specify what system he wanted, he said that Labour would at the next general election commit to a new system where "everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard".

Under a move to any more proportional system, on current trends, there would likely be more Green MPs as a result. In the scenario of a hung parliament, the Greens are a party to which Labour would naturally look for support as part of the progressive bloc.

And yet the Greens are also now a party whose actions this weekend have been condemned by the Labour chair, Bridget Phillipson, as "shameful" and "fundamentally wrong". Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, said the Zionism motion "crosses a line and is rightly being condemned across the political spectrum."

Labour has long been divided on the question of electoral reform. Their leader now has a clear position in favour but the Green motion this weekend could have the unintended effect of bolstering opposition within Labour to that element of the prime minister's agenda.

Bottles of water and sweets poking fun at Andy Burnham were handed out at the Conservative Party conference

Published 5 October 2026

An artist has said he is taking legal advice after accusing the Conservative Party of copying his portrait of Andy Burnham at their party conference.

People attending the event in Birmingham have been handed water bottles featuring the image and labelled "Bottler Burnham" and "0% strength" and sweets labelled "Andy Panders' People Pleaser Pick N Mix".

Labour supporter Stanley Chow, who created the image for Burnham's 2021 mayoral campaign in Greater Manchester, has claimed the party did not ask for permission to use the image.

A Conservative Party spokeswoman said the bottles were not on sale and merely handed out to attending media in "goody bags".

Manchester illustrator Chow said: "I was stunned and angry when I saw what they had done. It is childish from them. I am taking legal advice.

"I'm very disappointed. It's frustrating that an institution like the Conservative Party has no idea that they are infringing copyright."

The original image of Andy Burnham was created by Chow in 2021

The artist claimed Reform UK had also infringed his copyright by using the image a few months ago in AI-generated social media campaign posts.

A Reform UK spokesman said at the time that it had "removed the posts in good faith and without any admission of liability on our part".

Brit Awards art trail turns streets into a gallery Published 19 February

'Simple shapes and sweeping curves' Published 11 April 2014

Meet Stanley Chow - the football illustrator. Video, 00:02:35 Meet Stanley Chow - the football illustrator Published 7 November 2018

Chow said: "I can't quite believe the Tories are resorting to this too.

"Regardless of your political allegiance, what the Tories have done is still copyright infringement.

"Ultimately, I want to raise awareness that you can't just take someone else's artwork and do what you want with it.

"I want to show other artists that when this does happen, you can make a stand, especially in this day and age where artists are struggling, because of AI and the cost of living."

Chow's image of Burnham has been used extensively by the politician across a series of campaigns and was recently used by the now-PM when he stood for election in Makerfield in June.

Chow's image of Burnham was widely-used in the Makerfield by-election in June

Manchester United fan Chow is well-known for his portraits of famous faces and he has previously created images of footballers, including Wayne Rooney, Edgar Davids and Ronaldinho.

He has also exhibited a series of portraits of "Great Northerners", which featured the likes of actress Maxine Peake, suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst and poet Lemn Sissay, and recently curated an art trail for the Brit Awards' arrival in his home city.

He has also drawn Eric Cantona and presented a picture of Sir Alex Ferguson to the former Red Devils manager.

stories.title: Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion
stories.summary: The motion, which has divided senior party figures, backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein said the motion "crosses a line"

Published 5 October 2026

The chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein has told the BBC it is "quite possible" she will leave the party after Green members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.

The motion, which has divided senior party figures, also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It has been condemned by some Jewish groups and Israel's foreign ministry.

Asked by BBC Radio 4's Today programme about her future, Lichtenstein said: "I haven't decided yet...It is quite possible that I will leave the party...I'm giving it a little time and to talk with colleagues."

Lichtenstein, who is a former chair of her local party, said she had opposed the motion from the first time she heard about it.

"I don't think it's helpful and it doesn't make any difference whatsoever to Palestinians in Gaza who have suffered devastation, orphans left behind, it doesn't make any difference to Palestinians in the West Bank who are currently suffering, are currently being attacked and killed."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813.

There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.

The party's leader Zack Polanski, who is himself Jewish, had called for the motion to be amended to add in protections for Jewish members and remove language referring to a "single democratic Palestinian State". Both of these amendments were defeated.

Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on either this or the substantive motion. He left early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a by-election to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here .

The motion, among other statements, "supports the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants".

It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it".

Lichtenstein said she defines herself as "both Zionist and anti-Zionist" depending on the definition, and said a problem with the motion is that there are many definitions.

She said she was not concerned about "people accusing me of supporting Israel's right to exist and therefore I'm a racist, which of course is not the case", but said the "very bad motion...crosses a line".

One way in which it did that, she said, was that the proposers said they had consulted some Jews, but did not consult the Jewish Greens, who would have made some amendments to improve the motion.

She said there was a "vast range" of opinions among Jewish Greens, some who supported the motion entirely, others who supported aspects, and others who were against it. Some Jewish Greens also support one state, she added.

She said that party policy was that "it's up to Israelis and Palestinians to choose their future - one state or two".

Last month, the UK and 11 allies reiterated their support for a two-state solution , which would recognise a Palestinian state alongside an Israeli one. Israel rejects a two-state solution.

Her concern with the motion was that the Green Party may accuse UK, Israeli, or Jewish organisations, including those that partner with Palestinians, of racism. She said she supports many of these groups working "against the occupation and even go out on the ground to assist Palestinians".

She said she knows of some non-Jews who are planning on not staying in the party because "they think the motion crosses a line" and also because of their work, if they might not be able to be associated with a party that has "Zionism is racism" as a policy.

Asked whether she believed there were antisemites inside the party, including at senior levels, she said "there are certainly some antisemites in the party, I don't know about at senior level, that is not my experience".

The motion was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813

In response to the motion, Israel's foreign ministry said it had banned Polanski from entering the country.

A Green spokeswoman insisted the party would protect Jewish members - and they would not be persecuted for attending synagogues which defined themselves as Zionist.

Speaking after the vote, Lubna Speitan, the Green member behind the motion, argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression".

"We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions," she added.

Four of the party's five MPs - Ellie Chowns, Adrian Ramsay, Carla Denyer, and Sian Berry - had publicly opposed it, but the leadership was divided.

In her interview on the Today programme on Friday, co-deputy leader Rachel Millward had called the motion "problematic", while her counterpart Mothin Ali told the BBC on Saturday he would support the motion in its original form.

The Movement for Progressive Judaism, one of the largest and most liberal strands of Judaism in the UK, released a statement condemning the motion, which it said was "antisemitic in its formulation and intention".

"Jewish self-determination is a right. Declaring it racist is an attack on Jews," the statement read.

Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis also called the motion "poisonous antisemitism, a threat to British Jews and to Britain".

The Green Party motion said it "rejects attempts" to - among other things - "equate anti-Zionism with antisemitism" and said "we affirm that definitions of anti-Jewish discrimination should not equate Jewish identity with Zionist ideology or political practice".

Opposition parties pushed back against the motion.

Labour chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said the vote "crosses a line" and called on Polanski to "make clear that this will not be their position moving forwards".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp criticised the motion on behalf of the Conservatives, saying it demonstrated the Green Party was "toxic to its core".

Liberal Democrat MP Luke Taylor said the "divisive" motion did not address "the rising threats" of Islamophobia and antisemitism in the UK.

stories.title: Asos confirms hackers sent 'unauthorised' notification to app users
stories.summary: Asos confirmed an "unauthorised customer notification" was sent out via its app on Tuesday, after users raised alarm.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 6 October 2026, 10:49 BST

Asos says it is investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms it uses after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers .

Dozens of people told the BBC they received the strange "ASOS HACKED" message from the clothing and beauty store's app on Tuesday morning - with some saying it left them "scared" to open the app.

The notification was addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT teams in what cyber security experts said looked like a "brazen" extortion attempt.

Asos acknowledged the "unauthorised customer notification" on Tuesday afternoon, saying some "basic personal information" may have been accessed.

In an email to customers on Tuesday night, the company apologised and urged customers not to engage with the notification. And it said the website and app are "operating as usual" promising customers they can "shop with confidence" while it investigates the incident.

The company has not as of yet informed the UK's data watchdog, the Information Commission's Office (ICO), about any breach.

Exactly how many Asos customers received the notification on Tuesday remains unclear, but Google's Play store says the ASOS app has been downloaded to android devices more than 10 million times.

The British retailer has a substantial global footprint - serving around 17 million customers each year across more than 150 markets.

Some Asos app users in Australia, France, Sweden and the Republic of Ireland had also received the notification, according to local reports on Tuesday.

Hackers seeking to pile pressure on potential victims by informing their customers is rare, as most extortions happen in private, so this incident may go down as a significant moment in cyber-attack history.

Shares in the company fell by around a tenth on Tuesday.

Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, called it a "deeply serious" and "brazen" attack whereby the hackers had apparently "turned Asos' own app into their ransom note".

But she told the BBC that Asos customers should not be "scared and frightened" - encouraging those worried to change their passwords, avoid clicking on the notification's link and be cautious about possible scam emails or texts.

M&S cyber-attack disruption to last until July Published 21 May 2025

Extortion message

The message popped up on many Asos app users' home screens on Tuesday morning

Users of the Asos app appeared to have received the alarming notification at around 10:00 BST on Tuesday.

Headlined "ASOS HACKED" and addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT teams, it said: "We have fully compromised the Snowflake instance."

"Engage with us, or we will leak it," it added, before linking to a Telegram channel.

The message left many ASOS customers confused.

"At first I thought it was an ad or a fun promotion like 'ASOS HACKED get 50% off everything for a limited time only'," Jodie, an analyst from Edinburgh, told the BBC.

"Then I read the rest of the message which clearly showed that it wasn't an ad and instead a message to IT."

Jodie's concerns about what the Asos incident might mean for data she has shared with the platform, like her address, are shared by other users

"My main concern is that my information, such as bank information, home address, telephone number, has been compromised," said Erin, a student at the University of Sheffield.

She told the BBC that while her friends have expressed similar concerns about a potential data leak, her sister did not receive the notification on the Asos app.

"So the question is what is the extent? Are all customers affected even if they didn't get the notification? It's poor from Asos on all fronts."

Asos said in its statement that it took "immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms" on Tuesday - adding it was working with specialists within and outside the company, as well as relevant authorities.

It said it does not believe payment-card information or account passwords were impacted, and that its site and app are "operating as normal".

"Customer trust is incredibly important to us, and if the situation changes an update will be provided as appropriate," it said.

The BBC understands the National Cyber Security Centre has offered assistance to Asos.

Meanwhile Snowflake - whose tools are used by dozens of firms to collect, analyse and store data - told the BBC its investigation was ongoing, but it had so far found "no compromise" of its platform.

The company's services have, however, been the subject of many high profile data breaches in recent years.

Snowflake has previously been linked to cyber incidents targeting Ticketmaster and Santander.

According to cybersecurity expert Jen Ellis, Snowflake collects data from multiple sources for analysis, and an "enormous" firm like Asos will have lots of data about how people shop globally.

However Dan Bird, from cybersecurity firm Horizon3, said the message implied the apparent hackers' access had gone beyond the Snowflake database.

"Sending a push notification to Asos's app users would require access to the company's notification system, which is separate from the Snowflake data platform the attackers claim to have compromised," he said.

"If both claims hold up, it suggests the attackers got hold of credentials that opened more than one door."

What can I do to protect myself?

The company has also shared a statement , external to the London Stock Exchange's Regulatory News Service, which provides updates to investors.

Cybersecurity experts, including Ellis, have told the BBC those behind those behind this incident are most likely trying to "apply pressure" to Asos to meet their demands, rather than target its customers.

While those who received this notification will undoubtedly be concerned, it is important to know that it does not mean your phone has been hacked.

We are still waiting to find out exactly what "basic personal information" may have been impacted in this incident, if any.

But for now, the advice is:

Do not click on links in the notification

Visit Asos's official website directly for updates

Watch out for emails, texts or calls offering refunds, compensation or help with your account - scammers will exploit this type of incident when they know people are worried

Try and use different passwords for your online services

Enable two-step verification on email and banking accounts

Keep an eye on your online transactions for anything unusual

stories.title: Roll-out begins for passport-free airport e-gates
stories.summary: The system uses facial technology to check travellers against immigration and passport information.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The new system will be 25% faster than having to show your passport, officials said

Published 44 minutes ago

Passengers arriving into the UK will be able to pass through airport e-gates without showing their passport under a new contactless system, the government has announced.

On Tuesday, East Midlands Airport became the first airport to offer the new technology before it is rolled out to all UK airports by early 2027, the Home Office said.

The system uses facial technology so as passengers approach the e-gate, their photo is taken and then checked against immigration, travel and passport information and, if verfied, the barrier opens automatically.

Testing showed the new contactless system was up to 25% faster than using a passport, according to officials.

If further checks are needed, travellers will need to put their passport on the reader or may be directed to a Border Force officer.

Officers will continue to monitor all e-gates and offer assistance, while passengers should keep their passport with them at all times, the Home Office said.

East Midlands Airport said they expected a 'smoother, swifter and simpler' passenger experience

Phil Douglas, director general of Border Force, said: "This is a win for travellers coming to our brilliant country.

"By using state-of-the-art technology, we are making journeys smoother and faster, all while fully maintaining the UK's robust border security.

"Our digital transformation also builds on our work this summer to extend eGates to children aged eight and above, making life a little easier for families."

Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, the trade body for the country's airports, said the move was "excellent news for the passenger".

She added: "It is vital that we have the fast, efficient borders that arrivals into the UK now expect, and we will work closely with our members and government officials to ensure a smooth rollout."

Steve Griffiths, managing director of East Midlands Airport, in Castle Donington, Leicestershire, said: "We're delighted to be the first UK airport to have contactless e-gates introduced by Border Force.

"As an airport committed to providing an effortless travel experience, we welcome any technological innovation that can help to safely make our customers' journeys smoother, swifter and simpler.

"This complements changes that we carried out to our immigration hall recently to help improve the flow of arriving passengers through the area."

Standard e-gates are currently available at Birmingham, Bristol, Cardiff, East Midlands, Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, Heathrow, London City, Luton, Manchester, Newcastle and Stansted.

stories.title: 'Don't axe Youth Parliament' pleads teen member
stories.summary: The government plans to no longer fund the scheme launched to get young people into politics.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Aman Fatima has been a Member of Youth Parliament for two years

Published 5 October 2026

A taxpayer-funded programme aimed at boosting young people's interest in politics should not be axed just because "money is tight", one of its members has said.

Last month the BBC learned the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) would not be committing to giving any more grants to the UK Youth Parliament.

"If the government is to cut the Youth Parliament there should be reasons and there has to be alternatives, even if the funding is tight," Aman Fatima, MYP for Essex, told BBC Politics East.

The government said it was working on a new scheme to increase young people's involvement in democracy and decision-making, with further announcements due this autumn.

Established in 1999, the parliament takes place at the House of Commons and boasts more than 300 elected members aged between 11 and 18, including Aman.

She said if the scheme – run by the National Youth Agency – was scrapped, an alternative must be found because "young people are the next generation" of government.

"Money is tight but you also want young people's opinions; them to tell you what's wrong and the challenges they are facing," she said.

"And the [Youth Parliament] really helps young people get their voice out there, especially in a big place such as the House of Commons."

Members of the UK Youth Parliament, formed in 1999, hold an annual debate within in the House of Commons every year

As part of the programme, the young politicians are allowed to hold debates in the House of Commons chamber, on a day when MPs are not sitting, once a year.

In recent years, they have campaigned on issues such as votes for 16-year-olds and for free period products to be made available to students.

"There are lots of opinions from people saying that they haven't seen any difference made, but I think we do contribute to how the government works today," added Aman.

In the last year, the youth parliament received £453,000 in taxpayer funding with about £2.4m public money spent on it between 2017 and 2024.

No final decision has been made on funding after March 2027, but a government source said Downing Street would no longer commit to it "in its current form."

Labour MP Jess Asato believes there are other ways for young people to make their mark in politics

Jess Asato, Labour MP for Lowestoft, said she believed the decision had been made because the Youth Parliament was not producing "a diversity of voices".

"I think what the government's trying to say is we need things much more locally that bring a lot more young people into that political or democratic engagement," she said.

"In East Suffolk we have a fantastic youth council and that means lots and lots more young people can get involved in things that they care about locally.

"But I do wish the government might look at this [decision] again."

Conservative MP Patrick Spencer said funding for Labour government's plans had to come from somewhere

Patrick Spencer, Conservative MP for Central Suffolk and North Ipswich, said: "The reality is this government needs to make cuts because it needs to fund things that it's planning to do.

"It's one of the difficult decisions that has got to be made."

The DCMS praised the youth parliament's "important legacy" and said it had given elected young people "a national platform to represent their peers, engage with decision-makers and develop confidence, leadership and skills for life and work".

stories.title: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
stories.summary: The merger of two of Hollywood's biggest movie studios comes after months of legal disputes and concern over competition.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 6 October 2026, 13:55 BST

Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape.

The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers.

It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory.

The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network.

Paramount will acquire ownership of iconic franchises that include Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Lord of the Rings to add to its existing catalogue of hit franchises which includes Indiana Jones, Mission: Impossible and Shrek.

The newly merged entertainment behemoth will be re-branded under the name Skydance Corporation, the company originally founded by David Ellison before he took over both Paramount and Warner Bros Discover.

Ellison, chairman and chief executive of Skydance, said the completion of the deal was "historic" for the film industry.

"From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality," he said.

Films and streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you Published 5 hours ago

Last week, Ellison named the outgoing chief executive of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-chief executive.

Kreiz will focus on the company's day-to-day operations, including integrating the newly-combined businesses, while Ellison will focus on strategy and technology.

Mark Thompson - who once served as director general of the BBC - will continue in his role as chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN Worldwide, while Bari Weiss remains editor-in-chief of CBS News.

Casey Bloys, who has lead HBO and Max Content, will be the co-chair and chief content officer for direct-to-consumer content.

Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said that change "essentially means the HBO leadership team is now in charge of Skydance's combined streaming operation".

"While that bodes well for the HBO brand, make no mistake, Bloys will be pressured to find and deliver cost efficiencies that could affect content quality," he warned.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said the company has high debts at a time when interest rates are high.

"The combined entity, now called Skydance, needs to cut costs and make bigger profits to be able to get the debt down to more manageable levels," he said.

"The fact Tom Cruise movie Digger, Warner Bros' last release before the merger, has been a major flop is a reminder of how the film industry is not a guaranteed ticket to riches."

Rocky path to merger

While the company said it had received unanimous approval from competition authorities across the world, the long running takeover process has featured controversy since the beginning.

Netflix initially had a deal to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery, but Paramount Skydance launched a bidding war, leading to the streaming giant walking away.

Lawyers in about a dozen US states then filed lawsuits - led by California - aiming to block the deal, arguing it would stifle competition, raise consumer prices and cause "substantial" harm to movie theatres, cable distributors and "ultimately, audiences nationwide".

US states announced a settlement with Paramount and Ellison last month which paved the way for the merger to go ahead .

As part of the deal, Paramount has agreed to establish a "news editorial independence board" to "ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting" at CNN and CBS.

Politics and editorial independence has become an area of concern at CBS since the news broadcaster was taken over in 2025 as part of separate a merger between Skydance Media and Paramount.

Ellison, who hosted a dinner for President Donald Trump earlier this year, has sought to reassure people that editorial independence will be maintained.

Over its 103-year-old history, Warner Bros has won more than 100 Academy Awards - including dominating at last year's show with a record-tying 11 Oscars for One Battle After Another, Sinners and Weapons.

Paramount traces its roots back 1912 and also boasts more than 100 Oscars for classics spanning from The Godfather to Titanic, though the studio has not mirrored the same recent spate of Hollywood honours.

The studio was not nominated for any projects last year by the Academy. Its last win came in 2022 with Top Gun: Maverick.

The deal with US states aims to ensure the merged studios will produce "real, robust movies" that will generate economic activity and put people back to work, said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the lawsuit and settlement.

To prevent the studio from fulfilling its annual quota with low-budget or automated content, the deal includes strict guardrails against "AI-generated" films.

As part of the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year. If it fails to meet its annual production quota, it will be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax, the film company founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein and his brother Bob.

Paramount also must ensure 20% of all film production takes place in the US for the first two years, rising to more than 30% through the following three years.

stories.body:
Trump supporters may be surprised to learn the state takeover of means of production is not driven by the left

Americans will never accept the Democratic party’s slide to the left, or so desperate Republicans are hoping.

With the midterm elections fast upon us, Zohran Mamdani’s promise of a few city-run bodegas in New York City will scare the bejeezus out of middle America. Disgust over the democratic socialists’ unicorn-and-puppy promises of a world without capitalism will keep the Republicans in power.

Leading the charge against the new reds-under-the-bed is Donald Trump. “Together, we will defeat communism,” Trump promised in his recent TV ads .

Trump’s supporters might be surprised to discover that the United States is, indeed, sliding in the direction of a command and control economy. But the state takeover of the means of production is not being driven by the left. The grab for the US’s productive resources is the project of none other than Trump – who, it’s a fair guess, has never read Lenin.

The latest evidence comes in data crunched by the V-Dem project in Sweden, which measures the erosion of democracy around the world. It built a scale to gauge “state ownership of the economy”. As noted by Cullen Hendrix from the Peterson Institute for International Economics, from 2002 to 2024, the US ranked among the four countries with the least state control. In 2025, the first year of Trump’s second term, it dropped from second place to 16th.

By November of last year, the Trump administration had spent more than $10bn taking stakes in companies he deemed essential for national security, from Intel to a range of ventures mining for critical minerals. It also acquired an option to take a stake in Westinghouse, which makes nuclear reactors. And it blackmailed Nippon Steel into granting Trump’s Washington a “golden share” in exchange for the go-ahead to purchase US Steel.

To be fair, Trump’s acquisitiveness notwithstanding, the US is not even close to flirting with the flavor of socialism favored by the Soviet Union and its satellites in the second half of the 20th century. By the V-Dem accounting, Washington’s stake in the economy is still smaller than in 163 countries.

Government-run companies are a standard feature in many market economies. The Norwegian government has a majority stake in its massive oil company, which puts the country in 18th place. Even “communist” countries are pretty capitalist: private companies contribute 60% of China’s GDP .

And in a geopolitical landscape shaped by competition with China, there is a reasonable case to be made for Washington to take equity stakes in industries that are critical for American leadership and security, and which might not develop autonomously in competition with rivals heavily subsidized by Beijing.

Yet Trump’s wanton lunge for private assets lacks the discipline required for this kind of strategic positioning.

The president’s statist leanings mark a dramatic break with the market-focused presidencies of his recent predecessors, Democrat and Republican. The question is, what motivates him? His appetites are embedded in a body of thought that is skeptical, if not outright hostile, towards essential building blocks of the global market economy. He has pushed back against globalization since his first term in office, seemingly drawn to the Marxist-inspired dependency theory , which washed across Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s proposing protectionism and state industrial policy as a path to economic development.

His lust to control the economy is there for all to see. Though the supreme court already slapped down his attempt to take over trade policy from Congress, he is still threatening to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT”. His promise to give $5,000 to every American if Republicans maintain control of Congress in November’s elections underscores how he views the state’s coffers as his private piggy bank. Even his commie-bashing ads were paid for by taxpayer dollars.

Still, he clearly has no interest in the dictatorship of the proletariat, caring little if at all for the fate of the downtrodden. His preferred flavor of redistribution takes from those on the bottom to give to those on the top.

If anything, Trump reminds us that socialism is not the only ideological justification for state projects to take control over resources and wealth.

Watching the US president bow to Xi Jinping last week, it’s tempting to think that Trump wants to emulate China’s leader. Xi gets to rule unimpeded over more than one billion Chinese. He gets to shape China’s society and economy at will – purging this rival, raising that sycophant to power.

But Xi’s China is too disciplined for Trump. The Chinese leader still relies on hordes of technocrats to execute a coherent strategy aimed to achieve technological superiority. The US president doesn’t have the attention span for this kind of thing.

Rather, Trump’s model might be Vladimir Putin, who rules Russia like a fiefdom. Or maybe one of those dictators the US used to support in Latin America during the cold war: Haiti’s Papa Doc Duvalier or Anastasio Somoza in Nicaragua, who saw government as a tool to enrich their families and cement dynasties in power. If nothing else, Trump’s dealings with crypto suggest he views his administration as a road to family riches.

Karl Marx may not be Trump’s guiding light. But his writings can help understand Trump’s place in history. Marx proposes that his tome The 18th Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, about the 1851 coup that brought Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte to power in France, was meant to “demonstrate how the class struggle in France created circumstances and relationships that made it possible for a grotesque mediocrity to play a hero’s part”.

Americans may be grateful that their most recent class struggles didn’t produce a homegrown Lenin. But they did deliver Donald Trump .

Perhaps this does not condemn the US to an autocratic future. Hendrix points out that while Trump “clearly wants to be king”, the US’s political economy may not let him. Putin managed to establish autocratic rule over a fairly primitive, oil-based economy. This kind of control “is much harder to achieve in a modern complex economy” such as that of the United States, Hendrix noted. You can’t simply seize the oil to run the place.

Though Trump may fail, Americans’ acquiescence as he grabs for power raises a question for those who freak out over Mamdani’s city-run bodegas: why is Trump’s lurch to take over the American economy any better than what they hear from the Democratic Socialists of America?

Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

stories.title: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
stories.summary: India’s toy shops provide an unlikely barometer by which to measure its economic relationship with China.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Xi and Modi have vowed to address growing trade imbalances

Published 5 October 2026

Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China.

Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%.

Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked.

Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market.

The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world.

Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year.

"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC.

More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period.

"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI).

If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava.

Anti-China sentiment hit a fever pitch post border skirmishes in 2020, but relations have now thawed

On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address , external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues".

But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC.

That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods.

To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones.

"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava.

It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment.

Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank.

"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production.

Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends.

China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output.

Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year.

A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava.

India has reduced smartphone imports but depends heavily on China for components

On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies.

"Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li.

"If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same."

The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava.

But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short.

India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds.

"Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India."

More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising.

"But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds.

"The key question is whether Beijing is ready and willing to make concessions on market access as part of the broader normalisation. Alternatively, India will need to find its own leverage to force that conversation."
